section_summary: This section closes a history of Japanese teachers’ unions with a chronology, bibliography, and list of interviews. It then contains U.S. political adviser despatches on printers’ facilities and penalties in labor disputes, a trade-union petition seeking relief for punished workers, and the opening portion of a Japanese government statistical report on labor unions at the end of 1947.

subfiles.title: A History of Teachers’ Unions in Japan
subfiles.about: The closing pages document teachers’ union activity and identify the report’s written and interview sources.
subfiles.summary: The final chronology covers protests over Iwama’s arrest, disputes about teachers’ bargaining and strike rights, wage negotiations, and preparations for the February 1947 general strike, which SCAP prohibited. A bibliography and a dated list of conferences identify newspapers, union documents, government publications, and interviewees used for the history.

subfiles.title: Prefectural Survey of Printing Facilities of Members of the Japan Printers Union
subfiles.from: Acting U.S. Political Adviser for Japan
subfiles.about: Forwards two copies of a Civil Information and Education Section survey of printers’ facilities.
subfiles.summary: Despatch No. 300 encloses two copies of the April 13, 1948 survey.

subfiles.title: Disciplinary Action in Labor Disputes
subfiles.from: W. J. Sebald, U.S. Political Adviser for Japan
subfiles.about: Transmits a Labor Division memorandum and union petition concerning penalties imposed during labor disputes.
subfiles.summary: Sebald summarizes complaints about penalties and the Labor Division’s view that Japan’s democratic institutions can address alleged infringements of labor rights.

subfiles.title: Disciplinary Action in Labor Disputes
subfiles.from: James S. Killen, Chief, Labor Division
subfiles.about: Reviews punishments arising from communications, finance, printing, and manufacturing labor disputes.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum describes provost-court sentences after telegraph lines were cut, sanctions against finance workers, and Japanese court action against union production control. Killen concludes that Occupation authority justified the provost-court action and that Japanese democratic processes should address other disputed penalties.

subfiles.title: Supplication to General Douglas MacArthur
subfiles.from: Liaison Council of All Trade Unions of Japan
subfiles.about: Requests acquittals, lighter sentences, and release of workers punished or detained during labor disputes.
subfiles.summary: The council argues that penalties and arrests obstruct free labor unions and Japan’s democratization.

subfiles.title: Department of State Charge Slip
subfiles.about: Records the charge of a document associated with labor-union file references.
subfiles.summary: A partially legible charge slip lists file references and Nicholson.

subfiles.title: Labor Union Survey Report, December 1947
subfiles.from: Japanese Ministry of Labor, Labor Statistics and Research Bureau
subfiles.about: Reports the nationwide labor-union survey conducted at the end of December 1947.
subfiles.summary: The report’s introduction states that Japan had 28,013 unions and 6,268,432 union members at the end of 1947 and compares those figures with June 1947. It describes distribution by industry, prefecture, sex, formation date, union size, organization, agreements, dues, staff, and affiliated services. Survey instructions and blank forms precede statistical tables; the tables in this section begin with prefectural and industrial counts and continue through affiliation with national federations. The report continues beyond page 123.
